turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it’s Saturday, the nineteenth of September. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let’s go.
Today: a movement takes the second chokepoint, and the oil price falls anyway.
[curious] Falls? With both gates in one hand?
Third session running. And the pepper mill you own turns out to be a cutting tool wearing a decorative body.
[amused] That is either a metaphor or a kitchen story.
Both. It’s the spine: the narrow part. Two straits. One burr. A coat of sizing a few microns thick on a sheet of paper.
And twelve minutes a week, which I’m told is now the whole of my exercise obligation.
Saturday, so — the Scoreboard. Thirty-nine claims graded, and the one that stings is ours.
For three issues running we called gold at around four thousand three hundred dollars an ounce record territory. It wasn’t. The all-time high is about five thousand six hundred, set in late January.
[exhales] So we printed a drawdown as a record.
Three times. Friday’s print was four thousand three hundred and seventy-seven — twenty-two per cent below the high. A one-week high, and the first weekly gain in four. That is all it is.
[wry] The ledger outranks memory. Even when the memory is ours.
The Gulf. Day two hundred and two.
Last weekend we reported Saudi crude escaping the Strait of Hormuz by changing ships off Oman. That escape route runs out through the Bab el-Mandeb.
And over four days this month the Houthis took the whole Yemeni coastline that commands it. Zuqar and Mocha on the tenth. Mayyun — the island the charts call Perim — on the eleventh.
So the bypass and the blockade are now the same piece of water.
And the pipeline that makes the bypass work?

Drones hit a pumping station on the tenth. The kingdom shut the whole line — seven hundred and forty-five miles — the next day. About half of its seven-million-barrel capacity is back within days. The rest in roughly six weeks.
[thoughtful] And the war stopped being a proxy war.

A Houthi drone was intercepted over Taif on Thursday and the debris killed a man on Saudi soil. A second, aimed at Mecca, was brought down. Saudi aircraft struck telecoms towers in Taiz, killing a civilian; three children died elsewhere in the same exchange.
Here’s the line that travels. An adviser to Iran’s supreme leader: now the Iranians don’t only control Hormuz, they control the other most strategic chokepoint in the Middle East.
Twelve per cent of world trade passes a strait held by a movement making that promise.
The genuinely new thing: Reuters reports, on three Iranian sources, that Beijing has privately pressed Tehran to rein the Houthis in — and the request came to Beijing from Riyadh.

Commerzbank raised its year-end Brent forecast to eighty-five — still eighteen dollars below Friday’s print — on transit volumes recovering. And a war-studies academic says the Houthis are terrible at governance and unlikely to hold a blockade for long.
[deadpan] The market is voting with them. December Brent closed below the front month.
The curve is pricing the disruption out. We aren’t — but we print that we might be wrong.
Second World story: the moment a system stops being watched.
On Wednesday the Security Council failed to renew the panel of experts monitoring sanctions on Iran. Eleven in favour. China and Russia against, which was enough.
What dies isn’t surveillance. It’s the record of surveillance — the thing that would tell anyone, later, what moved and where.
Then the Baltic. An Italian NATO fighter shot down a drone over Lithuania, and it was carrying an explosive device. Most likely entered from Belarus.
[thoughtful] And here we argue with ourselves. Two incidents four days apart invite one narrative, and the narrative may be doing work the facts don’t support.
And Gaza. Twenty-one killed when a building collapsed in Gaza City on Wednesday; on Friday a second roof caved in.
A refugee-council worker gives the sentence that explains the toll: people are choosing to stay in dangerous buildings, because the idea of living in a tent is worse.
[thoughtful] A year after the shooting mostly stopped, the mechanism killing people in Gaza City is masonry.
Home. The air cleared overnight.
At four this morning the twenty-four-hour index read seventy-nine in Central. Moderate in all five bands for the first time in a week. But look at the shape of Friday.

The twenty-four-hour index read its worst at midnight, when the one-hour particulate reading was around twenty micrograms. And it sat inside Moderate at five in the afternoon — the precise hour the one-hour reading peaked at sixty-one.
[curious] So the number that triggers purifiers in classrooms lags the air in your lungs by most of a day.
The other Friday story will outlast the weather: Waymo licensed as the country’s third autonomous-vehicle operator.
Vehicles within months, a manual-driving phase through next year, commercial rides in twenty twenty-eight. First domain is Labrador and HarbourFront.
And the question an engineer asks, from a user called buffybuffy — can this vehicle react to a traffic marshaller, and a sinkhole?
[laughs] That is the whole sceptic in one line.

The headline is a ninety-four per cent reduction in injury-causing crashes, from two hundred and twenty million miles. And Waymo says the quiet part on its own safety page — there is no perfect apples-to-apples comparison available today.

Add the geography. Not expressways. Not a monsoon squall. Not a lane of motorcycles filtering at a Bukit Merah junction at six in the evening. The familiarisation year isn’t a formality — it’s the whole experiment.
[excited] Right. The pepper mill.
A peppercorn is a dried drupe. Hard, brittle, full of oil held in cells. You want to fracture it, not smear it.
And the metal at its centre is the only part that decides whether it works. Peugeot’s mechanism is the reference, and the order of operations is the lesson.
The teeth are cut into the steel first. Then the steel is case-hardened — carbon driven into the surface, so the tooth faces are glass-hard while the core stays tough enough not to shatter.
And a supermarket burr?
Pressed from soft sheet and never hardened. Its teeth are folded metal, not cut edges.
Salt needs ceramic instead — chemistry, not marketing. Dissolved in moisture, salt is an electrolyte. It pits steel. Stainless included.

CrushGrind invented the ceramic mechanism in nineteen ninety-four, names its customers, and has more than eighty million mills carrying it. A company in Taipei advertises private label and logo printing — and names nobody.
And the Singapore clause, which I did not expect to find in a warranty document.
[amused] Among Peugeot’s warranty exclusions sits the phrase extended humid storage.
Buy acrylic, stainless or cast iron. Not beech.

Two test kitchens, independently, and neither picks the expensive one. The two-hundred-dollar mill carries a five-year warranty. The sixty-nine-dollar Peugeot carries an unlimited guarantee on the mechanism.
[wry] And the salt mill?
Skip it. Salt doesn’t go stale, grinding flaked salt destroys the flake you paid for, and CrushGrind’s own guidance says don’t grind wet salt.
Technology. Huawei, in Shanghai, Thursday.

The interesting announcement wasn’t the chip. It was the cabling. The new supercluster replaces forty-eight thousand optical modules with five and a half thousand optical engines — removing, they say, more than five hundred and fifty kilowatts from the interconnect alone.

Huawei can’t buy the leading lithography node. So it attacks every part of the system that isn’t the transistor. If each accelerator is behind, make the interconnect good enough that more of them behave like one machine.
And the sceptic is one line from a China analyst: the chip is coming way earlier, but the supercluster they announced is much smaller.

They can’t make enough. Prices on the current accelerator went up sixty per cent citing tight supply. One customer alone plans more than a hundred and sixty thousand chips — more than current capacity.
[deadpan] A faster roadmap into a fixed packaging ceiling is a schedule, not a supply.
And the chatter? There wasn’t any. Two submissions of this news drew seven points and no comments, and one point and no comments.
[chuckles] The most expensive launch of the week, and nobody turned up.
Which sets up The Kit. Apple’s new Mac Studio reaches Singapore on Tuesday, from three thousand four hundred and ninety-nine dollars. Limit two per customer.

Five hundred and twelve gigabytes of unified memory in a pool the graphics processor sees directly. For anyone running models locally, memory capacity — not compute — has been the binding constraint for two years.
[pause] And it doesn’t ship until late October.

And there is no independent measured review of this computer. None. We demoted a pair of headphones for exactly this reason last week; the rule holds when the product is one the desk would like to recommend.
Give me the sceptic in one move.
The same week, someone squeezed a twenty-seven-billion-parameter model into just under six gigabytes and kept ninety-eight per cent of its score.
If the frontier is learning to fit into the memory people already own, a machine whose whole proposition is memory capacity is buying insurance against a constraint that’s actively loosening.
[thoughtful] But only one of them costs eight thousand dollars. And only one can be tested tonight for the price of a download.
Good Life, briefly. A turntable with no motor touching the record.

The motor that turns the record is also a machine that vibrates, and the stylus can’t tell the difference between vibration and music. Esoteric’s answer is to remove the contact entirely — the platter is pulled round by induced magnetic force, with nothing touching it.
Fifty thousand US dollars with the arm.
[deadpan] And now the one number both makers choose to print.
Esoteric specifies wow and flutter at nought point nought six per cent. A Technics deck at five thousand dollars specifies nought point nought two five.
So the cheap one claims better than twice as good, on the only number they both publish.
Screen and Sound, and we were wrong-footed in an interesting way.

Friday we reported Resident Evil opening at three different percentages with no audience number. That number now exists — ninety-two, against ninety-six from a hundred and sixty-nine critics. The gap we expected didn’t appear.
[wry] And the sceptic is aimed at us. We’ve spent issues treating the critic-versus-audience gap as a diagnostic. The temptation now is to treat the absence of a gap as evidence of quality. It isn’t.
Print the count beside the score, or the score is doing work it can’t support.
Family Desk. A genuinely good natural experiment.
A South Australian reform accidentally ran the study everyone needed — two different age cohorts started secondary school in the same month. Twenty thousand students, seven waves of census data.
Which is the finding. It’s the transition, not the year of birth. And it lasts two years.
Set that against how transition support is delivered here — orientation front-loaded into the first week. One school’s programme ran across three days in January.
[thoughtful] Three days of welcome against an effect measured in years.

One more, a null result wearing good news. Six hundred and seventy-six adolescents, a branded anxiety protocol against ordinary progressive relaxation. Both arms improved. No significant difference on the primary outcomes.
They attribute it to common therapeutic factors — structured adult attention, emotional validation, the experience of being heard.
Macro. Tokyo raised rates, and the governor said out loud what the week was about.
The Bank of Japan went to around one and a quarter per cent. Highest since nineteen ninety-five, two days after the Fed moved.
Asked why so many central banks were tightening at once, he answered: they all seem to be responding to similar factors. For one, it’s inflationary pressure from the Middle East conflict.
There’s your spine. Two straits, and a policy rate in Tokyo.
Then the inversion. Last week yields rose because oil rose. On Friday Brent fell a third straight session and the whole US curve rose anyway.
The tightening is now in the system independently of the shock that caused it.
[excited] Rabbit Hole. Urban sketching — and it turns into a story about proof.
A Flickr group started in Seattle in two thousand and seven. Now a nonprofit, at five hundred and ninety-nine chapters worldwide.
What makes it a movement rather than a hashtag is an eight-point manifesto the community treats as a constitution. Draw on location. A record of time and place. Be truthful to the scene you witness.
[thoughtful] Read those three together and something odd happens.
They locate the truth of a drawing not in how accurately it resembles the thing — but in the fact that a person sat in front of the thing for forty minutes.

Which stopped being abstract in April. Hasselblad unveiled seventy finalists for its Masters award. Within a day a street-category frame was flagged as generative — a Coca-Cola bottle with impossible typography. By mid-May it was disqualified.
[pause] A sketchbook cannot be prompted.
The manifesto is, functionally, this hobby’s proof-of-humanity protocol — written eighteen years before it was needed.
The most expensive thing in a watercolour kit is usually the paint. The thing that decides what the paint can do is a treatment a few microns thick on the surface of the paper.

In the maker’s own words, the aim of sizing is to make the paper more resistant to liquid absorption. It’s why you can lift and scrub on good paper and can’t on cheap paper. And almost nobody selling you paint will mention it.
And the Singapore version is a different craft, not a complaint.
The first is the denominator. Eleven million reels under one hashtag. That’s what a beginner grades their third drawing against.
And the second: a teacher ran the blind test, and lost.
An instructor who sells watercolour courses for a living published four of her own sketches — some student-grade paint, some professional — and asked readers which was which.
[curious] How many got it right?
Two.
[laughs] Two.
Read honestly — the audience could not see the difference. The painter could feel it.
[thoughtful] That is the truest sentence available about this entire gear ladder.
Fitness. Twelve minutes a week, if they’re the right twelve minutes.
The largest pooled accelerometer dataset yet assembled. A hundred and forty-seven thousand adults, seven days of device-measured movement each.

A hundred and fifty minutes a week of moderate activity carried a hazard ratio of nought point seven. The same association appeared at roughly five hundred and ten minutes of light — or about twelve minutes of vigorous.
[excited] Forty to one.
Now the real sceptic, which is the field arguing with itself.

The same month, the European cardiology body published a statement whose opening is a demolition. Observational data suggest activity lowers mortality — however, this was not confirmed by randomised controlled trials.
[pause] And one author is on both documents.
So the community that produced this month’s large mortality number is on record, this month, saying mortality is the wrong outcome.
And the recruitment. One cohort’s baseline response was fifteen point six per cent. The other’s was five point five.
[deadpan] Those aren’t populations. Those are the fifth and the twentieth of people who said yes.

The honest synthesis is narrow and still useful. The direction is consistent. The absolute numbers are not to be trusted. And the one robust finding is that intensity does more per minute than duration.
A reason to go harder for a quarter of an hour. Not a reason to buy a lab test.
Travel Desk. The trophy and the loss arrived in the same quarter.
Singapore Airlines named the world’s best again on Friday, for the sixth year running. And it posted a seventy-six-million-dollar net loss on record revenue.
Those two facts are the same fact. Net fuel cost up seventy-eight and a half per cent — a nearly billion-dollar increase the airline attributes directly to the Middle East conflict.
And Changi has stopped growing. Passengers through July up one-tenth of one per cent. Meanwhile airfreight over the same period is up eight and a half per cent.
An airport whose passenger number is flat while its cargo number climbs is an airport in a fuel-price economy.
The Grand Tour — and I love that we led with the bad news. Three of the postcards are currently false. Go anyway, and go in six weeks.
The eight-arch bridge at Sanxiantai is closed to the public, and doesn’t reopen until the end of next year. Corroded girders, cracked piers, salt.
What’s left is the best of it. A coast road with nothing built on one side. A valley that turns gold twice a year. And a seawater hot spring on Green Island that’s one of only three in the world.

And a sceptic on the dark skies. Taiwan has exactly one certified dark-sky park, and it’s on the other side of the island. The association’s own chairman listed the six best stargazing sites, and this county and both its islands were all absent.
And The Table, where we’re covering a restaurant that hasn’t served a paying meal.
Johanne Siy’s own place at last. Twenty-six seats. And the buzz is nothing, because there can be none — no reviews, because nobody has eaten there.
Which we’ll say rather than dress up: too new to call. Book the counter now, eat in October, and judge it then.
[thoughtful] The Long Read. Japan. And the sentence that should stop you isn’t about money.
A writer watching primary-school children trade stickers in February recorded one saying to another: that sticker’s rate doesn’t match, so I can’t trade.
Rate.

The product is a five-hundred-yen sticker sheet, made by a ninety-seven-person company in Osaka, launched in March of twenty twenty-four. By last December, cumulative shipments had reached fifteen million sheets. By late June, thirty-four million.

Three things. First, purchasing power. Demand didn’t come from the stated target of preschool girls — it came from women now in their twenties and thirties who traded stickers as children, and are now solvent.
The company’s own release quotes one: back then I agonised over spending my meagre pocket money. Now I can buy as much as I like with an adult’s means.
Pocket-money prices met salaried demand. And the pocket-money side lost.
Liquidity. Two big resale platforms supply continuous public price quotation. Five-hundred-yen sheets reported moving at two to five thousand, with one reported outlier at a hundred thousand.

A site, explicitly unofficial, publishes a sortable rate ranking by series, derived from the platforms’ own trading data. Plus a buy-back price board, a lottery tracker, and stock listings for all forty-seven prefectures.
[exhales] That is a financial-data vendor for a children’s toy.
And it’s what the children are reading when they say a rate doesn’t match.

Retail broke first. In late January a chain opened pre-orders and the servers fell over within seconds. On the first of February a Shibuya store suspended sales for, quote, customer safety and trouble prevention. Three days later the chain suspended three whole series across every store.
And then the schools, because no regulator came. Public primary schools sent emergency notices banning the stickers, citing money disputes and bullying.
This month a reporter found shelves marked down from five hundred yen to a hundred. An eighty per cent cut, and children walking past it.

Here’s the argument. Japan has built a resale and price-discovery apparatus so complete, so cheap and so fast that it can convert almost any consumer good into a speculative asset within weeks — and destroy whatever social function the good had.
And a five-hundred-yen sticker is the proof precisely because it’s trivial.
The thing it destroyed was a children’s gift economy that had run on asymmetric generosity for two generations.
Japan has done this before, and how it ended last time is the most useful fact in the story.

In nineteen eighty-five a confectioner put a sticker inside a thirty-yen chocolate wafer. Thirteen to thirty-three million units a month at peak. Children bought the chocolate for the sticker and threw the chocolate away.
[pause] And this time, the regulator is absent.

Japan’s only anti-scalping statute covers event tickets. So the enforcement burden has migrated to the marketplace — which has already accepted the role, with pre-emptive listing bans on a games console, then fast-food toys, then this week on unopened trading cards.
The company told its August results call that these restrictions helped drive growth. Marketplace value up almost fifteen per cent — its first double-digit rise in three years.
[scoffs] It has discovered it’s cheaper to be a regulator than to be regulated. And it’s monetising the role.
A listed company, not the fair trade commission, will decide which toys children may trade at a price.

Four arguments against this piece, and three land. The bubble didn’t burst, the copycats did. The timing is against us — a lottery ran on the fourth, and another opened the day before we went to press. And the maker has an order book of some thirty million units for the rest of the year.
And the strongest: that resale is just filling a gap between supply and demand — the resellers as clearing mechanism for a maker who under-produced by a factor of eight.
We don’t claim the boom is finished. We printed the hundred-yen markdown and the mid-September ballot in the same breath deliberately, because the contradiction is the story.
Whether these sheets trade at a hundred yen next spring or ten thousand — the site will still publish the rate. The marketplace will still decide what may be listed.
And children will still be saying that a rate doesn’t match.
[thoughtful] The mechanism outlives the product.
Somewhere in that apparatus is a parent who set out to buy their daughter a sticker, and came home having learned the word rate from her.
The Last Word. The narrow part.
A week of small things deciding large ones. Two stretches of water are now an input to the policy rate in Tokyo, and the governor said so out loud.
Huawei, unable to buy a lithography node, attacked the wires instead. And twelve minutes a week carried the same association as a hundred and fifty.
And the two we liked best, because nobody sells them to you. In a pepper mill the entire product is a burr you never see. The body is a handle.
In watercolour the paint gets the shelf space and the argument — and what decides whether you can lift a wash is a sizing agent a few microns thick.
A number. On a website. That the children could read.
[pause] Find the narrow part before you buy the rest of it.
That’s the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-eight pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
